headings.title: Introduction to the Vulva and Anatomical Overview
headings.content: The external female genitalia are collectively referred to as the **vulva** or the **pudendum**. These structures serve vital protective, sensory, and reproductive functions. Anatomically, the area extends from the mons pubis anteriorly to the anal verge posteriorly, and laterally to the genitocrural folds. A thorough understanding of this topography is essential for nursing students performing perineal care, catheterization, and postpartum assessments in Nigerian clinical practice.

headings.title: The Mons Pubis and Labia Majora
headings.content:
1. **Mons Pubis**: A rounded, fatty eminence situated directly over the pubic symphysis. After puberty, it becomes covered with coarse hair. Its primary function is to cushion the pubic bone during sexual intercourse.
2. **Labia Majora**: Two prominent, longitudinal cutaneous folds that extend backward from the mons pubis toward the perineum. They form the lateral boundaries of the vulvar cleft. The outer surfaces are pigmented and hair-bearing, while the inner surfaces are smooth and contain numerous sebaceous and sweat glands. They serve a protective role for the delicate internal structures lying between them.

headings.title: The Labia Minora and Interlabial Space
headings.content: The **labia minora** are two thin, hairless cutaneous folds located medial to the labia majora. Rich in nerve endings and blood vessels, they lack adipose tissue and contain numerous sebaceous glands. Anteriorly, each labium minus splits to form a fold over and under the clitoris, creating the **prepuce** and the **frenulum** of the clitoris. Posteriorly, the labia minora often merge to form a transverse ridge known as the **fourchette**, which can be easily lacerated during childbirth.

headings.title: The Clitoris: Anatomy and Physiological Role
headings.content: The **clitoris** is the primary female erectile organ, situated at the anterior junction of the labia minora. It consists of a glans, a body, and two crura that anchor to the pubic bones. Composed of highly sensitive erectile tissue, smooth muscle, and numerous sensory nerve endings, its sole function is sexual arousal. Because of its extreme vascularity and nerve density, any physical trauma or tearing in this region causes intense pain and profuse bleeding.

headings.title: The Vestibule and Associated Glands
headings.content:
The **vestibule** is the almond-shaped space enclosed by the labia minora laterally. It contains the external urethral orifice, the vaginal opening, and the openings of several exocrine glands.
- **Bartholin's Glands** (greater vestibular glands): Located posterolaterally to the vaginal opening, they secrete mucus to lubricate the vagina during sexual arousal.
- **Skene's Glands** (paraurethral glands): Situated near the lower end of the urethra, their ducts open into the vestibule and secrete fluid that contributes to lubrication.

headings.title: The Vaginal Orifice and Hymen
headings.content: The **vaginal orifice** lies in the posterior half of the vestibule. Partially closing this opening is the **hymen**, a thin mucosal membrane containing connective tissue and blood vessels. The hymen varies significantly in shape and elasticity among individuals; it can be annular, cribriform, or septate. Stretching or tearing of the hymen commonly occurs during first intercourse, tampon insertion, or vigorous physical activity, leaving small residual tags known as **carunculae hymenales**.

headings.title: Vascular Supply, Innervation, and Lymphatic Drainage
headings.content: The external genitalia boast a remarkably rich blood supply, primarily derived from the **internal pudendal artery**, a branch of the internal iliac artery. Venous return mirrors this arterial supply, draining into the internal iliac veins. Sensory innervation is supplied chiefly by the **pudendal nerve** (S2-S4), along with branches from the ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves. Lymphatic drainage from the vulva flows primarily to the **superficial inguinal lymph nodes**, a critical pathway to remember when assessing for lower extremity or pelvic infections, malignancies, or sexually transmitted infections.

headings.title: Clinical Significance and Nursing Assessment
headings.content: Nursing assessment of the external female reproductive organs requires professional sensitivity, proper lighting, and patient positioning (lithotomy or dorsal recumbent). Nurses inspect the vulva for signs of edema, erythema, lesions, lacerations, hematomas, or discharge. In Nigerian hospitals, postpartum perineal checks are routine to detect early hematoma formation or perineal wound dehiscence. Respecting patient privacy and maintaining clear communication are paramount during these intimate examinations to reduce anxiety and build trust.
